stem: A researcher places a strip of guinea pig ileum in an organ bath. Compound X causes a sustained contraction. Adding acetylcholinesterase to the bath does not reduce the contraction. Atropine abolishes it, but hexamethonium and tubocurarine do not.
oneliner: Experiment: ileum strip + compound X → sustained contraction, unchanged by acetylcholinesterase, abolished by atropine, not by hexamethonium or tubocurarine → which compound?
ask: Compound X is most likely which of the following?

whyNot.B: **Acetylcholine**: broken down by acetylcholinesterase, so the response would fade
whyNot.C: **Nicotine**: acts at nicotinic receptors, which hexamethonium would block
whyNot.D: **Succinylcholine**: acts on skeletal muscle nicotinic receptors, not on gut muscarinic receptors
whyNot.E: **Trimethaphan**: a ganglion blocker; it would not contract the gut

why: **Contraction resistant to cholinesterase and blocked only by atropine** = a **direct muscarinic agonist not hydrolyzed by cholinesterase**: **bethanechol**.

drug.name: Bethanechol
drug.how: Activates M3 receptors; resistant to acetylcholinesterase
drug.watch: Cholinergic effects: sweating, salivation, bradycardia, bronchospasm; avoid in asthma

chain: Gut and detrusor smooth muscle contract

stem: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis takes a new oral drug for joint pain. The drug is a weak acid with a pKa of 4.4. Gastric fluid pH is about 2, and plasma pH is 7.4. Her physician explains how the drug crosses gastric mucosa.
oneliner: 58F + rheumatoid arthritis + oral weak acid, pKa 4.4 + stomach pH 2, plasma pH 7.4 → ionization state?
ask: Which of the following best describes the drug in the stomach compared with plasma?

options.A: Mostly ionized in the stomach, mostly nonionized in plasma
options.E: Mostly nonionized in the stomach, mostly ionized in plasma

whyNot.A: This is a **weak base** pattern, not an acid
whyNot.B: pH 7.4 is **far above the pKa**, so the drug deprotonates in plasma
whyNot.C: At pH 2, which is **below the pKa**, the acid stays protonated
whyNot.D: Only at pH equal to the pKa (4.4) would it be half ionized

answer: Nonionized in stomach (pH below pKa), ionized in plasma (pH above pKa)
why: By **Henderson-Hasselbalch**, a **weak acid is protonated and nonionized when pH is below its pKa**. At pH 2 it is mostly **nonionized and lipid soluble**, so it crosses the gastric mucosa; at pH 7.4 it is mostly ionized (trapped).

drug.name: Weak acid drugs (e.g. aspirin, NSAIDs, phenobarbital)
drug.how: Nonionized form crosses membranes; ionized form is trapped in alkaline compartments
drug.watch: Alkalinizing urine traps weak acids (bicarbonate for salicylate or phenobarbital overdose)

stem: Researchers give a single oral dose of isoniazid to 500 healthy volunteers. Plasma concentrations measured 6 hours later, plotted as a histogram, form two distinct peaks, one at a low level and one at a high level, with few volunteers in between. The drug is cleared mainly by hepatic metabolism.
oneliner: Study: oral isoniazid in 500 volunteers + 6-h plasma levels show two distinct peaks → what explains the pattern?
ask: Which of the following best explains the bimodal distribution?

whyNot.B: **Renal secretion**: isoniazid is cleared by liver metabolism, as stated
whyNot.D: **Protein binding**: would give a continuous spread, not two groups
whyNot.E: **Gastric pH**: would alter absorption in a graded way, not two discrete groups

why: **Two discrete groups of drug levels** = a **genetic polymorphism**. Isoniazid is inactivated by **N-acetyltransferase**, so **slow acetylators** have high levels and **fast acetylators** have low levels.

drug.name: Isoniazid
drug.how: Blocks mycolic acid synthesis (needs KatG activation); inactivated by N-acetylation
drug.watch: Neuropathy and lupus-like syndrome (slow acetylators), hepatitis, give B6

stem: Two 65-year-old men of identical weight have MRSA bacteremia. Patient A has a glomerular filtration rate of 60 mL/min and patient B has a rate of 20 mL/min. Both will receive intravenous vancomycin.
oneliner: Two 65M, same weight + MRSA bacteremia + GFR 60 vs 20 + IV vancomycin → which parameter is the same?
ask: Which of the following will be the same for both patients?

options.C: Serum concentration 12 hours after the same dose

whyNot.A: **Half-life**: longer in B because clearance is lower
whyNot.B: **Time to steady state**: depends on half-life, so it is longer in B
whyNot.C: **Concentration at 12 h**: higher in B as less drug is cleared
whyNot.D: **Maintenance dose**: depends on clearance, so B needs less

answer: Loading dose (determined by volume of distribution, not clearance)
why: **Loading dose = target concentration × volume of distribution**, which is similar for patients of equal weight. **Clearance (kidney function)** alters the **maintenance dose, half-life and time to steady state**.

drug.name: Vancomycin
drug.how: Binds D-Ala-D-Ala, blocking peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis
drug.use: MRSA, C. difficile (oral), enterococci, serious gram-positive infections
drug.watch: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, red man syndrome (infusion rate), thrombophlebitis

stem: A 61-year-old man has sustained ventricular tachycardia 2 days after a myocardial infarction. He receives an intravenous lidocaine bolus and then a continuous infusion to keep the plasma concentration at a fixed target. The physician calculates the infusion rate from known pharmacokinetic values.
oneliner: 61M + VT 2 d after MI + lidocaine bolus then infusion to a fixed target concentration → infusion rate equals what?
ask: Which of the following determines the maintenance infusion rate at steady state?

whyNot.A: This gives the **loading dose**, not the infusion rate
whyNot.C: Wrong form; the rate **rises** as clearance or target rises, it is a product
whyNot.D: Not a formula for dosing rate

why: At steady state, **rate in = rate out**. Elimination rate is **clearance × concentration**, so **infusion rate = CL × Css**. The loading dose uses Vd × target.

drug.name: Lidocaine
drug.how: Blocks sodium channels, favoring depolarized or ischemic tissue
drug.use: Ventricular arrhythmias after MI, local anesthetic
drug.watch: CNS toxicity (seizures, tinnitus), bradycardia, high first-pass metabolism so given IV

stem: A 26-year-old healthy man receives an experimental beta-1 receptor drug in a pharmacology study. After the drug, his resting heart rate rises from 62 to 74/min, but his peak heart rate on a treadmill falls from 188 to 162/min. He has no other medical problems.
oneliner: 26M + healthy volunteer + beta-1 drug → resting HR 62 to 74 + peak exercise HR 188 to 162 → drug behaves how?
ask: Which of the following best describes this drug at the beta-1 receptor?

whyNot.A: **Full agonist**: would raise the heart rate further during exercise, not blunt it
whyNot.B: **Pure competitive antagonist**: would lower the resting heart rate, not raise it
whyNot.C: **Inverse agonist**: would reduce receptor activity at rest, so resting rate would fall
whyNot.E: **Noncompetitive antagonist**: would lower the resting rate and cannot add tone at rest

why: **Higher resting rate but blunted exercise rate** = partial agonist. At rest it adds some receptor stimulation; during exercise it **competes with high-level norepinephrine and epinephrine** and caps the response below the full agonist maximum.

drug.name: Pindolol / acebutolol
drug.class: Beta-blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (partial beta agonists)
drug.how: Weakly activate beta receptors while blocking full agonist binding
drug.watch: Less resting bradycardia than other beta-blockers; not used after MI

stem: A drug trial compares a new opioid with morphine on dose-response curves in the same tissue. Both act at the same receptor, and naloxone reverses both. At high doses the new drug's curve plateaus at a clearly lower maximal effect than morphine, even though increasing doses fully occupy the receptors.
oneliner: Dose-response study + new opioid vs morphine + same receptor + naloxone reverses both + plateau at lower maximal effect → drug acts how?
ask: Which of the following best describes the new opioid?

whyNot.A: **Full agonist with lower potency**: the curve shifts right but still reaches the **same maximum** as morphine
whyNot.B: **Competitive antagonist**: produces no effect by itself, so no curve of its own
whyNot.D: **Noncompetitive antagonist**: has no agonist effect alone, so it would not produce a dose-response curve
whyNot.E: **Inverse agonist**: lowers baseline receptor activity below normal, not a lower plateau of positive effect

why: **Same receptor, lower maximal effect despite full occupancy** = partial agonist (lower efficacy). Potency (curve position) and efficacy (maximum) are separate: **efficacy is reduced, not potency**.

drug.name: Buprenorphine
drug.how: High affinity, low intrinsic activity at mu receptors, so a ceiling on respiratory depression
drug.watch: Can precipitate withdrawal in patients on full agonists; ceiling effect on respiratory depression

stem: A 23-year-old woman develops a temperature of 40.1 C, a rigid jaw and stiff limbs 20 minutes after induction of general anesthesia with an inhaled agent for a knee arthroscopy. Her end-tidal CO2 is rising rapidly and her heart rate is 150/min. The anesthesiologist stops the inhaled agent and gives the specific antidote.
oneliner: 23F + rigidity, 40.1 C, rising end-tidal CO2 20 min after inhaled anesthetic + specific antidote given → antidote works how?
ask: The antidote relieves her condition mainly through which of the following actions?

options.A: Blocking nicotinic receptors at the motor endplate
options.B: Blocking calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
options.C: Preventing acetylcholine release from the motor neuron
options.E: Blocking voltage-gated sodium channels in the muscle membrane

whyNot.A: **Nicotinic blockers (curare, rocuronium)**: would relax muscle but do not stop the calcium-driven hypermetabolism; succinylcholine can even trigger the crisis
whyNot.C: **Botulinum toxin**: blocks ACh release, but the defect here is inside the muscle fiber
whyNot.D: **NSAIDs or acetaminophen**: this is not a hypothalamic fever; antipyretics do not work
whyNot.E: **Local anesthetics / antiepileptics**: block sodium channels, not the intracellular calcium release causing the contracture

answer: Blocking calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (dantrolene)
why: **Rigidity + hyperthermia + rising CO2 after an inhaled anesthetic** = malignant hyperthermia. **Dantrolene blocks the ryanodine receptor**, so less calcium leaves the sarcoplasmic reticulum and the sustained contraction and heat production stop.

drug.name: Dantrolene
drug.how: Binds the ryanodine receptor to block Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
drug.watch: Hepatotoxicity, muscle weakness

stem: In an anesthetized animal, a recording electrode on the phrenic nerve shows normal, rhythmic firing. After a test drug is given intravenously, the diaphragm stops contracting and no pressure change occurs in the abdomen, although phrenic firing and acetylcholine release at the junction are unchanged. Acetylcholine applied directly to the endplate no longer depolarizes it.
oneliner: Anesthetized animal + normal phrenic firing + normal ACh release + diaphragm stops + ACh at endplate no longer depolarizes → drug acts where?
ask: The drug most likely acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Competitively blocking nicotinic ACh receptors at the endplate
options.B: Blocking voltage-gated sodium channels in the phrenic axon
options.C: Inhibiting acetylcholine release from the nerve terminal
options.D: Activating mu opioid receptors in the brainstem
options.E: Enhancing GABA-A receptor activity in the CNS

whyNot.B: **Sodium channel blockers (lidocaine, tetrodotoxin)**: would abolish the phrenic firing, but firing is normal
whyNot.C: **Botulinum toxin**: would reduce ACh release, which is unchanged here
whyNot.D: **Opioids**: depress central respiratory drive and phrenic firing, not the endplate response
whyNot.E: **Barbiturates / benzodiazepines**: central depression would reduce phrenic firing

answer: Competitive nicotinic receptor blockade at the endplate (tubocurarine)
why: **Nerve firing and ACh release normal, but the endplate does not respond to ACh** = a postsynaptic block. **Tubocurarine competes with ACh at the nicotinic receptor**, so no endplate depolarization and the diaphragm is paralyzed.

drug.name: Tubocurarine
drug.how: Competitive antagonist of nicotinic ACh receptors at the motor endplate
drug.use: Muscle relaxation during surgery or intubation (class use)
drug.watch: Histamine release causing hypotension; reversed by neostigmine

stem: A 5-year-old boy is terrified of needles and needs a fast, smooth induction of anesthesia by mask before a dental procedure. The anesthesiologist chooses sevoflurane because it produces unconsciousness quickly.
oneliner: 5M + afraid of needles + mask induction wanted + sevoflurane chosen for rapid onset → which property explains it?
ask: The rapid onset of this agent is best explained by which of the following properties?

whyNot.A: **High blood solubility**: the blood acts as a reservoir, so equilibration is slow and onset delayed
whyNot.B: **High lipid solubility**: signals greater potency (low MAC), not faster onset
whyNot.D: **Low lipid solubility**: signals lower potency (high MAC), not speed
whyNot.E: **CSF solubility**: not the determinant of how quickly the alveolar concentration rises

why: **Rapid mask induction** depends on a fast rise in the brain partial pressure. A **low blood:gas partition coefficient** means little agent dissolves in blood, so alveolar and arterial partial pressures equilibrate quickly.

drug.name: Sevoflurane
drug.how: Low blood:gas solubility gives rapid induction and recovery
drug.use: General anesthesia, especially mask induction in children
drug.watch: Malignant hyperthermia trigger; decreased blood pressure; renal concerns from compound A

stem: A 28-year-old man is found unresponsive after injecting heroin, with a respiratory rate of 4/min and pinpoint pupils. He wakes and breathes normally within minutes of an intravenous injection of an antidote. Ninety minutes later, with no further drug use, he is again drowsy and his respiratory rate is 6/min.
oneliner: 28M + heroin overdose, RR 4 + woke after antidote + 90 min later drowsy again, RR 6 → why the relapse?
ask: Which of the following best explains the return of respiratory depression?

options.A: The antidote is a partial agonist at opioid receptors
options.B: The antidote has a shorter duration of action than the opioid
options.C: The antidote does not block the receptors heroin acts on
options.D: The antidote has a narrow therapeutic index
options.E: Tolerance develops quickly to the antidote

whyNot.A: **Partial agonist**: a partial agonist would not reverse overdose so completely and fast
whyNot.C: **Not blocking heroin's receptors**: he woke promptly, so the receptors were blocked
whyNot.D: **Narrow therapeutic index**: toxicity of the antidote is not the problem; his depression came back
whyNot.E: **Tolerance to the antidote**: tolerance does not develop within 90 minutes

answer: Antidote's half-life is shorter than the opioid's (naloxone)
why: **Quick rescue, then recurrence within 1-2 hours** = naloxone has a **short half-life** compared with heroin (and especially methadone), so the opioid outlasts the antagonist; patients need observation or repeat dosing.

drug.name: Naloxone
drug.how: Competitive mu receptor blocker with short duration of action (1-2 h)
drug.watch: Recurrent respiratory depression when the opioid outlasts it; withdrawal in dependent patients

stem: A 36-year-old painter develops blurred vision, headache and nausea after cleaning equipment with paint thinner in a closed room. Examination shows hyperemic optic discs. Arterial pH is 7.26 and the anion gap is 22. A drug is started that prevents formation of the toxic metabolite by acting on an enzyme.
oneliner: 36M painter + paint thinner in closed room + blurred vision, hyperemic discs + pH 7.26, gap 22 + antidote acts on an enzyme → which enzyme?
ask: The antidote works by inhibiting which of the following enzymes?

whyNot.A: **Aldehyde dehydrogenase**: inhibited by disulfiram, which would pile up acetaldehyde and not help here
whyNot.C: **Formaldehyde dehydrogenase**: inhibiting it would raise formaldehyde and worsen injury
whyNot.D: **Lactate dehydrogenase**: not involved in methanol metabolism
whyNot.E: **Pyruvate dehydrogenase**: not involved in methanol metabolism

why: **Optic disc hyperemia + high anion-gap acidosis after paint thinner** = methanol poisoning. **Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase**, so methanol is not converted to formaldehyde and formic acid and is cleared in the urine.

drug.name: Fomepizole
drug.how: Blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, stopping methanol and ethylene glycol activation
drug.watch: Headache, nausea, dizziness; no CNS depression

stem: A 38-year-old man presents 3 hours after drinking methanol. The preferred antidote is unavailable, so an intravenous infusion of ethanol is given. A laboratory study of alcohol dehydrogenase shows that in the presence of ethanol the apparent Km for methanol increases while the maximal velocity (Vmax) is unchanged.
oneliner: 38M + methanol ingestion + IV ethanol given + alcohol dehydrogenase Km for methanol up, Vmax unchanged → ethanol acts how?
ask: Which of the following best describes the action of ethanol in this setting?

options.E: Feedback regulator of formic acid synthesis

whyNot.A: **Noncompetitive inhibitor**: lowers Vmax with no change in Km
whyNot.B: **Allosteric activator**: would speed methanol conversion and worsen toxicity
whyNot.C: **Irreversible inactivator**: would lower Vmax, and ethanol is itself a substrate
whyNot.E: **Feedback regulator**: ethanol does not act on the downstream formic acid pathway

why: **Km up with unchanged Vmax** = competitive inhibition. Ethanol has a **higher affinity for alcohol dehydrogenase than methanol**, so it occupies the enzyme and less methanol is converted to formaldehyde and formic acid.

drug.name: Ethanol (as antidote)
drug.class: Alcohol; competitive substrate of alcohol dehydrogenase
drug.how: Competes with methanol and ethylene glycol for alcohol dehydrogenase
drug.use: Alternative antidote for toxic alcohol poisoning when fomepizole is unavailable
drug.watch: CNS depression, hypoglycemia; needs monitoring of ethanol level

stem: A researcher incubates purified acetylcholinesterase with diisopropyl fluorophosphate (DFP). Enzyme activity is lost and does not return after dialysis. Mass spectrometry of the inactivated enzyme shows a diisopropylphosphoryl group covalently attached to a single residue in the catalytic site.
oneliner: Purified acetylcholinesterase + DFP → activity lost, not restored by dialysis + diisopropylphosphoryl group covalently on one active-site residue → which residue?
ask: Which of the following amino acid residues is modified?

whyNot.A: **Histidine**: part of the catalytic triad but the phosphate group goes on the nucleophile
whyNot.B: **Cysteine**: not the nucleophile in acetylcholinesterase (that is serine)
whyNot.E: **Glutamate**: acidic member of the triad; not phosphorylated

why: **Irreversible loss of activity with a phosphoryl group at the catalytic site** = organophosphate inhibition. The drug **phosphorylates the active-site serine** (the nucleophile of the catalytic triad), so the enzyme is permanently blocked.

drug.name: Organophosphates (DFP)
drug.how: Covalently phosphorylate the serine in the acetylcholinesterase active site
drug.watch: Cholinergic excess; pralidoxime must be given before aging

stem: A 42-year-old woman is brought in after taking a large number of her husband's metoprolol tablets. Her heart rate is 38/min and blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg. Atropine and intravenous fluids produce little improvement. She is given an intravenous hormone that raises her heart rate to 78/min and blood pressure to 105/65 mm Hg within minutes.
oneliner: 42F + metoprolol overdose + HR 38, BP 70/40 + little response to atropine and fluids + IV hormone → HR 78, BP 105/65 → how does it work?
ask: The hormone restores her hemodynamics by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Blocking M2 muscarinic receptors in the sinoatrial node
options.C: Raising cAMP through its own Gs-coupled receptor
options.D: Opening potassium channels in the sinoatrial node
options.E: Direct agonist activity at beta-1 receptors

whyNot.A: **M2 blockade**: that is atropine's action, and it failed
whyNot.B: **Phosphodiesterase inhibition**: milrinone's mechanism, not a hormone effect
whyNot.D: **K+ channel opening**: would hyperpolarize the node and slow the heart
whyNot.E: **Direct beta-1 agonism**: the beta receptors are blocked by metoprolol; the hormone acts at a different receptor

answer: Own Gs receptor raises cAMP, bypassing the beta blockade (glucagon)
why: **Beta-blocker overdose resistant to atropine and fluids** is treated with **glucagon**. It binds its own **Gs-coupled receptor**, raising adenylyl cyclase activity and cAMP, so heart rate and contractility rise despite beta-receptor blockade.

drug.name: Glucagon
drug.how: Gs-coupled glucagon receptor increases adenylyl cyclase and cAMP in the heart (independent of beta receptors)
drug.watch: Nausea, hyperglycemia

stem: A 50-year-old man develops perioral tingling and numbness 30 minutes after eating a Japanese restaurant delicacy made from a spiny fish that inflates when threatened. This progresses to weakness, difficulty speaking and ascending paralysis, with a fall in blood pressure. He remains fully conscious but cannot breathe on his own. His pupils are fixed and dilated, and he has no fever or diarrhea.
oneliner: 50M + perioral tingling 30 min after restaurant delicacy + ascending paralysis, hypotension + conscious, apneic + no fever or diarrhea → toxin acts how?
ask: The toxin causes these findings by which of the following mechanisms?

whyNot.A: **Opening Ca2+ channels**: would increase excitation, not cause paralysis
whyNot.C: **Blocking K+ channels**: would prolong depolarization and cause excitation or arrhythmia
whyNot.D: **Opening Cl- channels**: would hyperpolarize neurons and cause sedation but not perioral numbness
whyNot.E: **Presynaptic ACh block (botulinum)**: occurs after improperly canned food, with descending paralysis, and does not cause paresthesias

why: **Perioral paresthesias soon after eating pufferfish, then ascending paralysis with preserved consciousness** = tetrodotoxin. It **plugs the voltage-gated sodium channel**, stopping action potentials in nerve and muscle.

drug.name: Tetrodotoxin
drug.how: Blocks the outer pore of voltage-gated sodium channels
drug.use: Not a therapeutic drug; foodborne poison
drug.watch: Perioral tingling, ascending paralysis, respiratory failure; supportive care only

stem: A 36-year-old woman has drooping eyelids and double vision that get worse by evening and better after rest. Her strength improves after she starts an oral drug. Measurements show that acetylcholine in her neuromuscular synapses rises.
oneliner: 36F + evening ptosis, diplopia, better with rest + oral drug → strength improves, synaptic ACh rises → how?
ask: How does the drug raise acetylcholine in the synapse?

options.D: Blocking choline uptake into the nerve terminal

whyNot.B: **Antimuscarinic**: blocks receptors, does not change the amount of acetylcholine
whyNot.C: **Direct agonist**: stimulates receptors but does not raise acetylcholine
whyNot.E: **Botulinum-like action**: would lower acetylcholine and worsen weakness

why: **Fatigable weakness, better with rest** = myasthenia gravis; **raising synaptic ACh** is done by a cholinesterase inhibitor that stops its breakdown.

drug.name: Pyridostigmine
drug.how: Inhibits acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine lasts longer in the synapse
drug.watch: Cholinergic excess: diarrhea, salivation, sweating, bradycardia, bronchospasm

stem: Volunteers receive increasing doses of morphine, and the percentage showing respiratory depression is plotted against dose. The experiment is repeated after pretreatment with naloxone.
oneliner: Volunteers + morphine dose vs % with respiratory depression → repeat after naloxone → how does the curve change?
ask: How does the dose-response curve change after naloxone?

options.A: Shift to the right with a lower maximum
options.D: Parallel shift to the right with the same maximum

whyNot.A: **Noncompetitive antagonism**: naloxone binds the same receptor reversibly, so a higher morphine dose can overcome it
whyNot.B: **Would mean more potency**; an antagonist cannot do this
whyNot.C: **Slope change** is not an effect of simple competition
whyNot.E: **Pretreatment with an antagonist** reduces morphine's effect at a given dose

answer: Parallel rightward shift with the same maximum (competitive antagonism)
why: **Naloxone competes with morphine at the mu receptor**: more morphine is needed for the same effect (higher EC50) but the **maximum can still be reached**.

drug.name: Naloxone
drug.how: Competes with opioids at the mu receptor; reversible
drug.use: Opioid overdose, reversal of respiratory depression
drug.watch: Precipitates withdrawal in dependent patients; short half-life, so overdose may return

chain: Competes with morphine at mu receptor

stem: A 66-year-old man in the coronary care unit has ventricular tachycardia after a myocardial infarction. The team wants to reach a therapeutic plasma concentration of lidocaine at once and will set the ongoing infusion later. The drug is given intravenously, so all of it reaches the circulation. A pharmacist asks which quantity defines the first dose.
oneliner: 66M + post-MI ventricular tachycardia + IV lidocaine + need target plasma level at once + maintenance set separately → which formula for the loading dose?
ask: Which of the following determines the loading dose?

whyNot.A: That is the **maintenance dose rate** (with F = 1 for IV), which replaces what is cleared
whyNot.B: Dimensionally meaningless; **clearance does not set the loading dose**
whyNot.C: Has the **concentration in the wrong place**; a higher target needs a bigger dose, not smaller
whyNot.E: That is the **half-life** formula, not a dose

why: The **loading dose fills the volume of distribution** to the target level: **Css × Vd (÷ F if not IV)**. It depends on **Vd, not clearance**. **Clearance sets the maintenance dose** (CL × Css), which replaces the drug eliminated.

drug.name: Lidocaine
drug.how: Blocks fast sodium channels in ischemic tissue; given IV with a load then infusion
drug.watch: CNS toxicity (tremor, seizures), bradycardia; clearance falls in heart failure and liver disease, so lower the infusion

chain: Fills the volume of distribution at once

idea.rule: Loading dose follows Vd; maintenance dose follows clearance.
also: Maintenance dose rate = CL × Css ÷ F
Renal or hepatic failure changes maintenance, not the loading dose

stem: A 47-year-old man with non-small cell lung cancer is about to receive high-dose cisplatin. He is given an antiemetic before the infusion that causes little sedation and no extrapyramidal effects. It acts on the chemoreceptor trigger zone and on vagal afferents in the gut.
oneliner: 47M + lung cancer starting cisplatin + antiemetic with no sedation or EPS + acts on trigger zone and gut vagal afferents → receptor blocked?
ask: Which receptor does this antiemetic block?

whyNot.A: Blocked by **metoclopramide and prochlorperazine**, which cause **extrapyramidal effects**
whyNot.B: Blocked by **scopolamine**, which causes sedation and dry mouth
whyNot.D: Blocked by **diphenhydramine and promethazine**, which are **sedating**
whyNot.E: **Activated** by dronabinol; it is an agonist, not a blocker

why: **Ondansetron** blocks **5-HT3 receptors** on the **chemoreceptor trigger zone and gut vagal afferents**, which cisplatin stimulates by releasing serotonin. It is **not sedating** and causes no extrapyramidal effects.

drug.name: Ondansetron
drug.how: Blocks 5-HT3 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and on gut vagal afferents
drug.watch: QT prolongation, constipation, headache

idea.rule: Chemotherapy-induced vomiting is treated with 5-HT3 blockers, often with NK1 blockers and dexamethasone.
also: Dexamethasone added for high-emetic regimens such as cisplatin
